The Search is on as Brother Poor Shifts Roles!
ijince I have never titled one of my col
umns, you may wonder why I am starting
now. The significance of the above head
line should not be lost on anyone inter
ested in the future of Psi Upsilon.
What this headline means is that the
Fraternity is about to embark upon a ma
jor step forward in its efforts to provide
the very best of service to our under
graduate chapters and members and at
the same time build the endowment of
The Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc. ,
so it
can achieve the educational aims con
sistent with its charter and supportive of
the Fraternity's primary educational
function.
This lengthy introduction will prepare
you for the shift in responsibdities for
Brother Henry B .
Poor, current Execu
tive Vice President ofthe Fraternity, who
will assume a new full-time position as
Executive Director of The Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc., on July 1, 1987. The
effect of this move is two-fold; (1) Brother
Poor's full-time attention to the Sesqui
centennial Fund Campaign aimed at im
proving the endowment of the Founda
tion will make it possible for the
Foundation to expand its support for the
Fraternity's educational programs and the
Foundation's scholarship program; and
(2) The Fraternity will be able to retain
access to Brother Poor's wealth of ex
perience while seeking a new chief ad
ministrative officer for the Fraternity.
In many respects, this is the best of all
possible worlds! The Foundation, which
has not had the full-time personnel to
actively pursue the Sesquicentennial
Fund Campaign, will now be able to fo
cus its efforts on the fundraising neces
sary to significantly increase its endow
ment and thus its long-term support for
appropriate Fraternity activities. At the
same time, the Fraternity will have an
opportunity to recruit a new chief ad
ministrative officer so that the level of
support for the Fraternity itself will re
main at the same high level enjoyed un
der Brother Poor's fine stewardship.
And so we must begin the arduous task
of seeking a new chief administrative of
ficer. What follows is the description of
the person we are seeking for the position
of chief administrative officer for the
Fraternity.
Yours in the Bonds,
William R. Robie

WE ARE FAMILY
(St. Louis, MO) College fraternities and
their role in higher education was the
focus of attention when the National In
terfratemity Conference (NIC) met from
December 4-7. Psi Upsilon was well rep
resented by William R. Robie, Epsilon
Omega '66, President of the Executive
Councd; Charles M. Hall, Nu Alpha '71,
Treasurer of the Executive Council; and
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, Executive
Vice President. Also in attendance were
Richard D. Dadey, Jr., Pi '80, and Carter
V. Forringer, Rho '84.
Representatives of Psi Upsilon at the
National Interfratemity Conference
meeting in St. Louis: Carter V. Forrin
ger, Rho '84; Richard D. Dadey, Jr., Pi
'80; William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega
'66; and Charles M. Hall, Nu Alpha '71
(Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, is missing
from the picture).
The theme of this year's meeting was
"We Are Family," and such a theme is
appropriate as the popularity and unity
of fraternities has never been stronger.
Fraternities have experienced rapid
growth, with over 400,000 undergradu
ates as members of 5,000 chapters and
colonies on 732 campuses across the
United States and Canada.
The NIC is an Indianapolis-based fed
eration of 59 national general college fra
ternities. It serves its member fraterni
ties in the areas of government,
university, and media relations. The
Conference also has a
policy-making
branch in the form of the annual House
of Delegates. In conjunction with the NIC
meeting, the Association of Fraternity
Advisors (AFA) also met. This group rep
resents the college and university ad
ministrators who have the responsibility
of working with fraternities on the cam
pus level.
TOMORROW THE WORLD (?)
(Paoli, PA) Psi Upsilon has a long tradi
tion of leadership on her campuses. Re
cently, when the staff was discussing In
terfratemity Council involvement, we
realized that this tradition is alive and
well today. At least four schools presently
have Psi U's heading their IFCs. These
schools are: University of Rochester
(Dennis Alport, Upsilon '88), Kenyon
College (Donald Dowd, Iota '88), Trinity
College (Rick McCaulley, Beta Beta '87),
and Tufts University (Steve Cheren, Zeta
Tau '87). In addition to these men, Psi
U in general seems to play an active role
in student government and leadership on
nearly every one of our thirty-three cam
puses.
NOW SHOWING
(Hollywood, CA) The highly-acclaimed
new movie, PLATOON, may owe some
of its success to Psi U. The film, a hard
hitting look at American soldiers in the
'Vietnam War, had as assistant to the di
rector Brother Evan Kopelson, Tau '87.
Evan, who worked for two months this
summer on location in the Philippines,
recounted the tribulations of the film crew
overseas. The peaceful revolution which
led to the ouster of Ferdinand Marcos
nearly forced the crew to move the shoot
ing to Thailand. Evan is considering en
tering the motion picture industry, fol
lowing the footsteps of his father, who
produced the film.

RAGS TO RICHES (AGAIN)
(Hamden, CT) One of Psi U's most pro
lific and most famous authors is about to
have yet another work published. Hor
atio Alger's (Alpha 1852) 104th book,
MABEL PARKER; OR, THE HIDDEN
TREASURE, originally scheduled for re
lease in 1878, should be in print by this
July. The erstwhile pubhshing company
of the novel suffered a very un-Algerian
(?) fate; shortly before its 1878 publica
tion date, the printer went bankrupt.
Now, 109 years later, it is to be put out
by the Shoe String Press of Hamden,
Connecticut. Let's hope for better luck
this time!

CALL
(Rochester, NY) In keeping with a new
experimental program at the University
of Rochester, one day a week part of the
Upsilon Chapter house is turned into a
classroom. On Wednesday afternoons,
students at the U of R have rearranged
their living quarters, not their life styles,
to accommodate residential courses and
their instructors. Viewed as a forum for
students who live together to learn in
formally, the new courses adjust to, and
develop along with, the dynamics of each
residence. On the first day of classes, the
Upsilon house was still being renovated.
Amidst the dust, drilling, two-by-fours,
and stereo music gathered a class of six
teen brothers and their instructor, Den
nis O'Brien, President of the University
of Rochester.
The course should be more beneficial
if there's the opportunity to discuss the
material over dinner, President O'Brien
told his students. "There's a greater
chance to learn the material, to refine it,
and to listen to its subtle inner voices."
He also noted that he considers the topic
of existentialism as "personally relevant"
and therefore ideal for the residential set
ting.
Students interviewed said they felt
more comfortable, willing to participate,
and were more inclined to attend a res
idential course than a course across cam
pus. Knowing one's classmates inti
mately, observed Upsilon Past President
Barry Rubio '87, prompted more people
to participate during the first class in ex
istentialism because "we already knew
each other and we weren't going to laugh
at others or judge them if they mis
spoke."
Brother Rubio said the relaxed class
setting was more conducive to learning
the material. He sees the residential
course as "something to share, an intel
lectual discussion between friends." He
added that class would be less competi
tive and didn't think his friends would
"worry as much about grades because they
just want to take advantage ofthis unique
opportunity."

but of a whole generation of politicians.

IN THE MOVIES
(Paoli, PA) A surprise to all of us occurred
recently when Psi U was mentioned on
the ABC mini-series "Monte Carlo." Ap

he fraternity chapter house �
few of us can imagine the college fraternity
without some form of living or meeting accommodations. In the very early
days of Psi Upsilon, however, fraternity houses did not exist. Meetings were
held in a member's room. In those days students lived primarily in private
rooming houses or with relatives who resided near the campus. Colleges
provided little, if any, housing for their students.
As early as 1844 at least one chapter of Psi Upsilon began renting
space to use for meetings and literary exercises. The first building
erected for a fraternity was by Chi Psi at the University of Michigan
in 1846. It was a one-room log cabin constructed by the members
in the forest near the campus. The structure was not used as a
residence but just as a meeting place for the members.
The first building constructed for Psi Upsilon was the mag
nificent Hall of the Beta in 1870. This building, too, was merely
a meeting place, commonly known in that era as "halls" or
"lodges" and sometimes "temples" or "tombs.
"
The Beta Hall
was undoubtedly one of the most impressive fraternity build
ings in the nation at the time of its construction.
Over one hundred years since this first building for Psi
Upsilon was constructed, over thirty-five houses or lodges
have been built for the fraternity. Today twenty-seven
of these still are standing, and seventeen of them still
are devoted to their original use �

Zeta, Kappa, Psi, Xi, Upsilon, Iota, Phi, Omega,
Pi, Chi, Eta, Tau, Omicron, Theta Theta. Zeta
Zeta, and Epsilon Omega. (Note: The home of
the Epsilon Nu Chapter actually was built for

The oldest of the twenty-seven
houses still standing is the "old" house
of the Psi Chapter at Hamilton Col
lege, built in 1885 down the street
from the "new" Psi Chapter house,
built in 1922. Now used as a private
home, the symbolic Psi Upsilon dia
mond still adorns the front of the
house, but the Psi Upsilon letters
have been replaced with those of
Lambda Chi Alpha, a reminder of its
most recent fraternity dweller.
The Beta Beta Chapter house at
Trinity College, built around 1880,
is the oldest of today's Psi Upsilon
houses. Constructed as a private res
idence, the Chapter purchased the
home in 1902, reportedly from the
former Governor of Connecticut. The
oldest house built for Psi Upsilon and
still in use by the fraternity is the Xi
Chapter house at Wesleyan Univer
sity, built in 1893.
In the late 1800s and early 1900s
an attitude of "keeping up with the
Jones'
"
prevailed among the chap
ters in the fraternity. The goal was
to build as large and imposing a house
as possible. Houses were being con
structed by very "young" chapters.
It is amazing to think that the funds
to build the magnificent houses of
the era were being raised by chapters
without large alumni bodies. The Tau
built its permanent home within eight
years of its installation as a chapter
of Psi Upsilon, the Omicron viathin
fourteen years, and the Theta Theta
within ten years.
The Kappa Alpha Society at Wil
liams College was, in 1864, the first
fraternity to have a residential house
for members. At many of the schools
where Psi Upsilon has chapters,
fraternity houses provided the only
housing for students. It was not until
after World War II that most colleges
began constructing modern dormi
tory facilities.
There is a broad range of architec
tural styles in Psi Upsilon's chapter
houses �
from the Greek revival of
the Theta and the Georgian revival
of the Upsilon and Chi to the tradi
tional New England homes of the
Zeta and Kappa; fi-om the revival Tu
dor of the Phi, Psi, and Theta Theta
to the contemporary homes of the
Zeta Zeta, Epsilon Omega, and Phi
Beta. All of these homes carry one
thing in common �
symbolic items
of the Fraternity are in evidence in
each. Coats-of-arms over doorways,
Greek letters in mantle pieces, owls
carved in pillars, stairways, doorways
or used as downspouts �
they all
mark their edifices as unmistakably
Psi Upsilon.

of articles featuring some of our more

providing an opportunity for all in Psi
Upsilon to experience the beauty and
distinctiveness of our chapters

PI CHAPTER HOUSE
Built 1891
J7 ormally dedicated on January 20, 1898,
the magnificent Pi Chapter house at Syr
acuse University was the first fraternity
house to be erected on that campus. The
home, which recently was listed on the
National Register of Historic Places, is
built in a Classic Revival style, with paired
doric columns symbolizing Greek archi
tecture, appropriate for a fraternity house.
Designed by Wellington P. Taber, Pi
1889, the large white house was origi
nally painted two colors �
the clap
boards a darker -hue with columns and
trim a lighter shade.
The surroundings of the house have
changed dramatically in the ninety years
since it was built. The campus has grown
from a few scattered buildings to the large
university that now literally surrounds the
house.
Though many delegations of Pi broth
ers have "trod these halls of yore," the
old halls have seen relatively few changes
over the years. The main floor remains
almost the same as when it was built. The
only major structural changes were the
addition of a dining room in 1904 and
repairs following a fire in 1907.
The large space on the first floor has
dark wood trim and beams. The walls are
lined with built-in seating upholstered in
red leather, with aged Oriental rugs grac
ing the floors. Numerous artifacts on the
walls lend an aura of fraternity.

Northern view of first floor circa 1913.
Southern view of first floor circa 1913.
The living room fireplace is
especially
interesting. The large brass screen bears
the Greek letters Psi and Upsilon on the
front panel, and the andirons are cen
tered with an owl whose eyes light up a
garnet color when a fire is burning. Over
the fireplace is the traditional founders'
plaque, with the Fraternity coat-of-arms
carved in wood on one side and the Pi
Chapter coat-of-arms on the other.
The stairway, which rises up through
the center of the house all the way to the
cupola on the roof (five stories in all), has
a domed stained glass ceiling. The eightsided dome represents the octagonal
badge of the Upsilon Kappa Society,
which was the precursor to the Pi Chap
ter. Centered in the dome is a replica of
the Psi Upsilon badge. At the landings
on the second and third floors the bal
ustrade curves outward, making an ideal
place for observation.
Originally the second floor was de
voted entirely to study rooms and the
third floor to dormitory space. The two
floors now contain fifteen single and dou
ble rooms, which combine sleeping and
study accommodations.
On the third floor a narrow stairway
leads to the two-story cupola. At the top
floor the view of the University below
and the City of Syracuse beyond is spec
tacular. When looking downward, one
sees the octagonal skyUght which is be
tween the third and fourth floors.
All who have visited the Pi house have
been impressed with its unique charm.
And the Pi brothers who have Uved in
this magnificent house have learned to
treasure it. We hope that others now can
appreciate the splendor of this landmark.

Fall has been a time for the Phi Beta

pus of William and Mary. We started the

ance and advice in our
attempt to furnish

September to make the house look good.

logos on some of the upstairs halls. We
also made some
temporary letters which
we mounted on the front of the house.

nor work, is finished, and we now have
long range plans to redecorate and fur
nish our basement into a
recreation/study
lounge.

year under Rush Chairman Michael
Senders '88. We pledged seven new
members last semester and look forward
to their initiation. Formal rush began at
the beginning of this semester, so our
numbers should increase by the time
spring arrives.

financially, thanks to our treasurer, Dave
Weaving '88. We hope to have all of our
outstanding debts paid off by the end of
this semester. Homecoming was a lot of
fun this year, considering that we actually
had alumni come back and visit. We en
tered a float and, although we did not
win a prize, those of us who participated
had a great time. In other social events,
besides our regular parties and some im
promptu ones, we had a great time. We
hosted a pajama party with the sisters of
Delta Gamma in October, which a lot of
our brothers enjoyed. Our semi-formal
in November was well attended and was
a nice change from the regular parties.

by the brothers.

alumni from various Chapters who made
donations to our Chapter for furnishings.
